content: The systematic review aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of tests for leprosy under programmatic conditions. Two key questions were addressed: whether there is a diagnostic test with sufficient sensitivity and specificity to diagnose leprosy (both paucibacillary [PB] and multibacillary [MB] forms) and whether such a test is feasible for use in programmatic settings. Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted using MEDLINE and Embase databases for studies published between 1996 and January 2017. The search strategy included MeSH terms and text words related to leprosy, diagnosis, sensitivity and specificity, predictive value, and diagnostic accuracy, combined using Boolean operators. No restrictions were applied regarding study design or language. Additional studies were identified by contacting experts in the field and reviewing reference lists of retrieved articles. All citations were exported to a reference manager for further analysis. Eligibility criteria included cohort studies, cross-sectional studies, and case-control studies that evaluated diagnostic accuracy against a reference standard. The population included adults and children suspected of having leprosy or confirmed leprosy patients, with non-leprosy controls also included. The reference standard for leprosy diagnosis was primarily based on the Ridley-Jopling (RJ) and WHO classifications, using clinical criteria with or without histopathological and bacteriological confirmation. Controls included household contacts, healthy individuals, and patients with tuberculosis (TB) or other skin conditions. The diagnostic tests evaluated included ELISA tests for antibodies to PGL-1, MMP-I and II, LID, and NDO; immunochromatographic/lateral flow tests; PCR; and other methods such as M. leprae particle agglutination and skin tests using M. leprae soluble antigens. Studies reporting sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, false positives, false negatives, or direct harms were included. Data extraction was performed using a standardized form, and a second reviewer checked a sample of studies for accuracy. Results: The search identified 568 citations, of which 73 full-text articles were reviewed. Ultimately, 40 studies met the inclusion criteria. The quality of evidence for all tests was rated as low or very low due to methodological limitations, including the use of case-control designs, lack of pre-specified test thresholds, and heterogeneity in patient classification (MB vs. PB) and control groups (household contacts, healthy controls, TB patients, etc.). Sensitivity and Specificity: ELISA tests showed high sensitivity for MB cases but low sensitivity for PB cases. Specificity was generally high across different control groups. PCR tests demonstrated higher accuracy than ELISA in some studies, particularly when using skin biopsy specimens. However, no study evaluated a commercially available PCR assay. Whole blood PCR (one study) showed sensitivity of 96% for MB and 70% for PB, with specificity ranging from 93% to 100%. Other tests, such as M. leprae particle agglutination and skin tests, showed variable sensitivity and specificity, with very low-quality evidence. Likelihood Ratios and Predictive Values: Likelihood ratios were calculated based on median sensitivity and specificity for healthy controls. Predictive values were estimated for hypothetical populations with different pre-test probabilities of leprosy (1%, 10%, and 20%). Limitations: Only two bibliographic databases were searched, though this was supplemented by expert input and reference list reviews. Some household contacts may have had undiagnosed or latent leprosy, complicating the interpretation of specificity when using this group as controls. The heterogeneity of study designs, populations, and diagnostic methods precluded meta-analysis. Conclusion: The evidence for the diagnostic accuracy of tests for leprosy is of low or very low quality. ELISA tests are highly specific but have limited sensitivity for PB cases. PCR tests show promise, particularly for MB cases, but their utility is limited by the need for skin biopsy specimens and the lack of standardized commercial assays. Further research is needed to develop and validate diagnostic tests with high sensitivity and specificity for both MB and PB leprosy, particularly those that are feasible for use in programmatic settings.
